title: South West Water fined almost £8m for sewage spills
description: A water company has been fined almost £8m for a series of pollution-related offences over six years.South West Water previously entered guilty pleas a
body: A water company has been fined almost £8m for a series of pollution-related offences over six years.South West Water previously entered guilty pleas at Plymouth Magistrates' Court after an investigation by the Environment Agency into incidents between 2015 and 2021 in Bodmin, Harlyn, Playing Place, and Polperro in Cornwall, and Plymouth in Devon.Of the 18 charges, 17 were for illegal discharge activities including sewage discharges and one is for failing to take reasonable remedial measures following a failure at a sewage pumping station. The firm was fined £7,867,733. The water company said in a statement after sentencing: "We apologise for what happened in the past."It said the case related to "historic matters between 2015 and 2021" and the majority of spills involved "the use of overflows in storm conditions"."We're investing £760m to tackle storm overflows and have reduced spills by 17% in the last year alone, with spill duration down by 25%," the company said.It added "significant improvements" had been made at the sites where pollution occurred."We remain focused on the future as we deliver record levels of investment to achieve cleaner rivers and seas across the South West by 2040, a decade ahead of national targets," it said.Follow BBC Cornwall on X, external, Facebook, external and Instagram, external. Follow BBC Devon on X, external, Facebook, external and Instagram, external. Send your story ideas to spotlight@bbc.co.uk, external.

schema.headline: South West Water fined almost £8m for sewage spills

title: Organised crime investigation sees 17 arrested in dawn raids
description: Police investigating a suspected organised crime group have arrested 17 people in dawn raids at 24 properties in London, Essex, Hertfordshire, Cambrid
body: Police investigating a suspected organised crime group have arrested 17 people in dawn raids at 24 properties in London, Essex, Hertfordshire, Cambridgeshire and Suffolk.More than 800 officers took part in the arrest operations in the early hours of  Tuesday.Searches are ongoing at a number of the properties and there is expected to be a police presence for some days, the Metropolitan Police said.An officer taking part in the operation in Cockfosters, Barnet, was stabbed in the leg while carrying out a warrant - his injuries are non-life changing.  The arrests were part of an investigation by the Met along with His Majesty's Revenue and Customs (HMRC) and the Financial Conduct Authority (FCA).The Met said the FCA has "disrupted" seven businesses and is "actively pursuing" another 30.A spokesperson said: "These arrests mark a significant point in this investigation."Those arrested are suspected of leading or being involved at a senior level in serious and organised crime and related financial offending."In total, 15 men aged between 26 and 65 were arrested, and two women aged 31 and 41.They are being held on suspicion of participating in the activities of an organised crime group, money laundering, cheating the public revenue, false accounting, and conspiracy to commit GBH.A 56-year-old man was also arrested on suspicion of GBH over the stabbing.Listen to the best of BBC Radio London on Sounds and follow BBC London on Facebook, external, X, external and Instagram, external. Send your story ideas to hello.bbclondon@bbc.co.uk, external

title: Sir Ranulph Fiennes: Relatives tell BBC it's 'very painful' not being able to visit him
description: Relatives of the British explorer Sir Ranulph Fiennes have said it is "very painful" he appears to have been hidden away from them. Speaking to BBC Ne
body: Relatives of the British explorer Sir Ranulph Fiennes have said it is "very painful" he appears to have been hidden away from them. Speaking to BBC Newsnight, his former sister-in-law told the BBC that she did not know where he was, and nobody had been able to see him.It has been alleged that Sir Ranulph, 82, has been admitted to a number of care homes under assumed names, after a family rift involving his second wife, Louise Millington-Cotes.Louise Millington-Cotes did not immediately respond to the allegations, or the BBC's request for comment.Cheshire Police have said they are aware of the concerns regarding Sir Ranulph, and are satisfied he is living in an appropriate setting with suitable care.They said there were "no immediate safeguarding concerns". Sir Ranulph has not been seen in public for nearly two years, just months after opening up about a diagnosis of Parkinson's disease. He was the first person to visit both north and south poles by surface means in the early 1980s and has been described by The Guinness Book of Records as "the world's greatest living explorer".Spending his childhood between the UK and South Africa, he joined the British Army after leaving school, going on to serve in the SAS.Sir Ranulph's stepson, Alex Millington-Cotes, told BBC Newsnight he wanted to see the power of attorney "removed from my own mother" and placed in the hands of people who "have fully his best interests in mind"."He's not an isolated type of person, and so to see him isolated now is very painful," he said. Questions about Sir Ranulph's whereabouts grew in prominence after a report in the Telegraph earlier this month, external in which "members of his inner circle" raised concerns about his whereabouts. Last week, he launched a crowdfunding campaign for legal fees to "locate and safeguard" the explorer. He wrote that the fundraiser had been created as "a result of our concern and desperation" after trying "multiple avenues" to locate his stepfather.Arabella Pepper, the younger sister of Sir Ranulph's late first wife Ginny, told BBC Newsnight that she had not been able to see her former brother-in-law for over a year. "All his friends and family want to see him and take him Toblerones and cheer him up, but we don't know where is, and he's not available, he's not accessible - that's what worries us," she said.She alleges that she was only able to see him in July 2025 after she admitted herself to a care home where she had been told he was staying. "The first thing I said to him, apart from the usual greetings, was that everybody was worried about him, was looking for him, was longing to see him," Pepper told the BBC."The relief on his face was very obvious, and he said, send a message to everybody, send them my love, tell them I love them and tell them I'm longing to see them."Posting on X, BBC world affairs editor John Simpson, wrote he was "horrified to hear what's happened to my good friend Ran Fiennes"."He's the world's bravest man, and he's vulnerable. We must know what's happening to him."Starting in 1967, Sir Ranulph has been the leader of almost 20 major expeditions, according to the Explorers Club.His expedition to both the north and south poles came during the Transglobe Expedition, in which he led the first team to circumnavigate the globe from north to south.Sir Ranulph has also enjoyed a career as a prolific travel writer, as well as authoring fiction, non-fiction and biographies.

schema.headline: Sir Ranulph Fiennes: Relatives tell BBC it's 'very painful' not being able to visit him

title: Argentina threatens legal action against UK over Falkland Islands oil exploration
description: Argentina's president has threatened to launch a legal challenge against the British government unless it halts oil exploration work off the coast of
body: Argentina's president has threatened to launch a legal challenge against the British government unless it halts oil exploration work off the coast of the Falkland Islands.In a social media post, President Javier Milei set a two-week deadline for the Sea Lion oilfield project, a joint venture between Israeli and British companies, to be scrapped.The companies insist they have valid licences issued by Britain.The comments heighten tensions between the UK and Argentina over the sovereignty of the archipelago, known in Argentina as Las Malvinas, more than 40 years after a British military task force ejected Argentine forces which had invaded the territory in 1982.Milei said that if the two-week deadline was not met, he had "instructed the Foreign Ministry and legal teams to initiate international arbitration" against the UK over what he called "the illegal plundering of our resources through the Sea Lion Project".He continued to warn the UK that if the "illegitimate exploitation" of the region didn't end within two weeks, Argentina would take the matter before the International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea.The International Tribunal is an independent judicial body based in Hamburg which is responsible for the fair application of the United Nations' Convention on the Law of the Sea.The move comes soon after Milei roundly criticised the UN in his speech at the General Assembly for failing to act over the sovereignty of the Falkland Islands.He said the UN had become "a useless organisation" which only serves "arrogant parasites dressed up as well-intentioned bureaucrats". Since then, the UK Defence Secretary, Wes Streeting, said that Argentina "lacks the ability" to seize the Falklands by force.

schema.headline: Argentina threatens legal action against UK over Falkland Islands oil exploration

title: Stormont future depends on Drumcree outcome
description: Politics in Northern Ireland is often accused of going nowhere fast but right now it more resembles a time warp taking us back three decades.Divisions
body: Politics in Northern Ireland is often accused of going nowhere fast but right now it more resembles a time warp taking us back three decades.Divisions that had been dormant over Drumcree flowed angrily again between the parties over the weekend, spilling over into Monday when MLAs returned to the chamber.Less than 24 hours after the secretary of state called on Stormont's leaders to "double down on compromise", what unfolded in the assembly was all double down, no compromise.Tempers and emotions flared - despite a warning from the Speaker, Edwin Poots, to mind their manners - amid shouting across the packed benches.Stormont is known for its theatrics but was what unfolded simply more performative politics or the warm-up for a dramatic act over devolution's future?Soon after, the Democratic Unionist Party (DUP) leader Gavin Robinson appeared to provide the answer as he gave a press conference on his party's next steps.He'd already warned that power sharing was in "difficult territory", as he hit out at First Minister Michelle O'Neill and other Sinn Féin politicians for taking part in the Garvaghy Road protest, and called for them to face prosecution.While saying then that it could not be "business as usual" at Stormont any more, the DUP leader went on to say he was not prepared to be reckless.From that we can take it to mean power sharing is going to carry on, for now.

schema.headline: Stormont future depends on Drumcree outcome

title: Evicted Spanish pensioner, Maricarmen Abascal, can move home, lawyer says
description: An evicted elderly disabled woman, who has become symbolic of Spain's housing crisis, will be able to return to her home in Madrid, according to her l
body: An evicted elderly disabled woman, who has become symbolic of Spain's housing crisis, will be able to return to her home in Madrid, according to her lawyer.Maricarmen Abascal, 87, was forcibly removed on a stretcher from her apartment of more than 70 years on 23 September. She was admitted to hospital after the eviction.Her eviction has led to widespread anger across Spain, and Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez has promised housing relief measures when his cabinet meets on Tuesday.Abascal's lawyer, Beatriz Duro, told a press conference there had been "goodwill from both parties" and that she would pay a similar amount of rent under a new contract, averting a significant price hike.Duro had met the investment company Urbagestión, which owns the apartment, for several hours on Monday, and the agreement they reached still has to be approved by Maricarmen Abascal, as she was unable to take part in the meeting.She added that Abascal, who is being treated for exhaustion, would sign the deal when she felt better.Up to 1,000 protesters welcomed the agreement at Madrid's Puerta del Sol, where hundreds of tents have been set up. However, the city's Tenants' Union has called on the government to approve deeper housing reforms "so that there are no more Maricarmens".The tent protest has been criticised by Madrid regional leader Isabel Díaz Ayuso, who has accused the government of failing to respond in time to Spain's housing shortage and of now coming up with "sectarian" and "deeply ideological" proposals."I'm merely asking to be told at what age I can stop paying my landlords so I can stay in my place, and maybe I'll even join the next tenants' protest," she said.Spain needed a million more homes to address demographic growth encouraged by the Sánchez government itself, she added.Maricarmen Abascal's father first rented the property in 1956 and she continued as the tenant after her parents died, during which time there was a cap on the rent.Urbagestión, which bought the property in 2018, increased the rent from €500 per month (£428; $572) to €2,650 (£2,280; $3,020). The company later offered to reduce this to €1,650 however she was still unable to pay this with her monthly pension of €1,350.Three previous attempts to evict her were blocked by the courts.Her case triggered nationwide protests and tens of thousands of people to march through the Spanish capital on Saturday to object to the eviction and to demand stronger protection for tenants in the face of a housing shortage and soaring rents.Duro said the agreement, yet to be signed, was the "result of the social mobilisation". Supporters called it a victory but promised to continue their fight to prevent similar evictions, and to press for more affordable housing.The Bank of Spain estimates the country is short of 700,000 homes, based on the gap between demand and new construction.House prices have risen by 12.2% in the past year, according to figures for the second quarter of 2026 from national statistics institute INE.The shortage in rental housing means that costs rose by 8.5% in 2025, according to real estate firm Idealista, with Madrid alone seeing an increase of 9.7% in rents. It said Barcelona and Madrid were Spain's most expensive cities to rent a home, at €23.8 per square metre (£20.4) and €22.7 per square metre respectively.Pedro Sánchez's Socialist Party, which lacks a majority in Parliament, is hoping to agree a new decree with his political allies to appease public outrage.A council of ministers was due to meet on Tuesday morning, with left-wing ministers calling for permanent protection for tenants.Negotiations went on through the night and the left-wing Catalan party ERC is said to have called for a halt to all evictions involving vulnerable people while also demanding a hike on taxes for tourist accommodation.In a speech on Monday evening, Sánchez promised that the government would act responsibly to tackle the "housing emergency suffered by so many people"."Patriotism also means preventing an 87-year-old woman from ending up on the street after a lifetime in her home," he said.

schema.headline: Evicted Spanish pensioner, Maricarmen Abascal, can move home, lawyer says

title: Fifa accuses Uefa of 'misinformation campaign'
description: Fifa has accused Uefa of a "misinformation campaign" and attempting to influence the race for its presidential campaign in new court documents.They al
body: Fifa has accused Uefa of a "misinformation campaign" and attempting to influence the race for its presidential campaign in new court documents.They also described Uefa's conduct as "in bad faith and for the purpose of harassment".Last month European football's governing body filed legal papers in the US requesting disclosure of evidence and documents from Fifa, warning it could lodge a criminal complaint in Switzerland.Uefa accused Fifa president Gianni Infantino of "criminal mismanagement" and "a fraudulently off-market price promoted by [him] for his own benefit" over the now-shelved Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE) scheme.In its response on Monday night, world governing body Fifa said Uefa's filing contained "numerous false or misleading statements about Fifa and Infantino"."With no basis whatsoever, Uefa suggests that Mr Infantino sought to profit personally from the FFE proposal," Fifa said in a filing in the Southern District of Florida, opposing Uefa's motion for discovery."Uefa's suggestions that Mr Infantino violated any law or ethical principle are categorically without merit."It also described Uefa's filing as "farcically overbroad" saying "districts faced with similar requests have outright rejected such applications".BBC Sport has contacted Uefa for comment. BBC Sport has been told insiders believe that if Fifa has nothing to hide, it should disclose the documents and speed up the legal process. Uefa has led the rebellion against the Fifa president, who is facing calls to stand down from three confederations.Fifa's FFE plan proposed selling stakes in the World Cup and other competitions to private investors, sparking a major backlash.Infantino faced calls for his resignation but claimed the project had been intended to generate additional money for the game.Earlier this month, Football Association chair Debbie Hewitt, a Fifa vice-president, told Infantino to release all documents relating to his controversial plan, and called for an independent review of FFE.Infantino will stand for election for a fourth time in March 2027, with his opponents having until 18 November to find an alternative candidate.

title: What is the triple lock and why are people talking about it?
description: Under the triple lock system, the state pension increases each April in line with whichever of three measures is the highest:inflation in the Septembe
body: Under the triple lock system, the state pension increases each April in line with whichever of three measures is the highest:inflation in the September of the previous year, using a measure called the Consumer Prices Index (CPI)the average increase in total wages, including bonuses, across the UK for May to July of the previous yearor 2.5%The rise in wages of 3.9% is likely to determine the April 2027 state pension increase.The triple lock was introduced by the Conservative-Liberal Democrat coalition government in 2010.It was designed to ensure the value of the state pension wasn't overtaken by the increase in the cost of living or the incomes of working people.The Labour government has previously said it would keep the triple lock until the end of the current Parliament.But since that commitment, there has been intense debate over the cost of the triple lock and whether it is justified.In July 2025, the government's official forecaster said the cost of the triple lock guarantee was set to be three times higher by the end of the decade than was originally anticipated when it began. The Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR) said the annual cost is set to reach £15.5bn by 2030.It said the cost of the state pension has risen steadily over the past eight decades, and now equates to £138bn, or around half the total amount the government spent on benefits.In July, the influential Institute for Fiscal Studies think-tank suggested that the triple lock should be scrapped as part of a wider pensions overhaul.There is now speculation that the government is considering ending the triple lock after the next general election as a way to fund a new social care plan.

schema.headline: What is the triple lock and why are people talking about it?

title: Lives will be lost unless UK does more to combat wildfires, committee chairwoman says
description: Image source, EPA/ShutterstockImage caption, The aftermath of a wildfire in Dunwich Heath, Suffolk, during the summerByAdrian Goldberg and Fergus Hewi
body: Image source, EPA/ShutterstockImage caption, The aftermath of a wildfire in Dunwich Heath, Suffolk, during the summerByAdrian Goldberg and Fergus HewisonFile on 4 InvestigatesLives "will be lost" unless more is done to combat the increasing risk of wildfires, the chairwoman of the UK's Climate Change Committee (CCC) has said after a record number of blazes this summer.Baroness Brown told BBC File on 4 Investigates "not enough action" had been taken in light of predictions the UK is facing longer, drier summers because of global warming.Earlier this year, one man died in a wildfire in Gloucestershire, while 19 homes were destroyed in Stourbridge, near Birmingham, and villagers were evacuated in the Cairngorms.The government said it was investing nearly £100m to improve national resilience capabilities, which includes piloting specially trained firefighting teams.UK 'not prepared for the changing climate'As far back as 2012, the independent CCC warned of "more frequent wildfires due to warmer and drier conditions". File on 4 Investigates has seen figures from the National Fire Chiefs Council showing that 2026 set a new all-time high, with 1,350 wildfires in England and Wales, up by more than 300 on last year and more than 1,000 on 2024. Records for the number of reported wildfires were also broken in 2022 and 2025. Baroness Brown said the CCC, formed in 2008, has been telling the government for years that the UK is "not prepared for the changing climate". She continued: "The warnings have been there and not enough action has been taken."I fear that lives will be lost. We need to be doing much more education and preparation."She said that included investing in specialist teams and equipment, but also "planning our woodlands, thinking about fire breaks" and early warning systems.By 2050, she said the risk of wildfires could be doubled across much of the UK. Tinderbox Britain - Are we ready for more wildfires?File on 4 Investigates looks at whether the country is prepared for the growing threat, and if the emergency services have the resources to cope.'No-one should have this experience'Uttam and Sandy Shiralkar are still coming to terms with the loss of their family home in Stourbridge after it was engulfed by a wildfire in August.Sandy, a surgeon, said: "We saw the complete destruction of the house. There was no roof, no floorboards. Nothing. No-one should have this experience."Image caption, Uttam and Sandy Shiralkar are now living in temporary accommodation after losing their family home in a wildfire... Image source, Uttam ShiralkarImage caption, ... their home was one of 19 destroyed in StourbridgeThe fires started accidentally in fields in Stourbridge, where farming machinery was in use on the hottest day of the year.The couple are now living in temporary accommodation. Uttam said: "Every loss is painful, but losing a house has got a different dimension. Coming back to normality is going to take a long time."Fire crews dangerously overstretched While the risk of wildfires is on the rise, the number of firefighters has been in decline.Steve Wright, general secretary of the Fire Brigades Union, which represents firefighters, said more than a fifth of firefighter and control room posts across the UK – some 12,000 jobs - had been cut since 2010, which left crews dangerously overstretched over the summer."We had firefighters from London being mobilised to Yorkshire, firefighters from Merseyside being mobilised to Dorset," he said. "The effect, when you have wildfires happening at the same time across the UK, is there's just not enough firefighters on the ground to be able to deal with them."Image caption, There are calls for more specialist training on how to tackle wildfiresPhil Garrigan, chairman of the National Fire Chiefs Council, which represents senior managers of the UK's fire and rescue services, said he welcomed the £97m investment to provide six specialist firefighting teams to work across the UK.But he insisted more money was needed to boost aerial firefighting capability and improve specialist equipment for firefighters. He said: "The money has to be there, otherwise we'll be going into 2027 and 2028 with a likely occurrence that we'll see what we've seen in 2026, which is 50 plus homes lost and families devastated by the impacts of wildfire. We've got to get ahead of that."State-of-the-art equipment such as dedicated off-road vehicles will be bought as part of the £97m investment, which the government said was funding the biggest upgrade to national resilience for 20 years.

schema.headline: Lives will be lost unless UK does more to combat wildfires, committee chairwoman says

title: 'Ship buster' missiles sink old US warship in live fire training off Scotland
description: Figure caption, The decommissioned USS Klakring was sunk at the Ministry of Defence's Hebrides rangeUpdated 13 minutes agoA decommissioned American wa
body: Figure caption, The decommissioned USS Klakring was sunk at the Ministry of Defence's Hebrides rangeUpdated 13 minutes agoA decommissioned American warship has been sunk off Scotland's west coast during a training exercise involving both US forces and the Royal Navy. USS Klakring was hit by missiles and a torpedo before sinking in the North Atlantic about 170 miles (274km) off the Outer Hebrides last Monday.The US Navy said the ship went a through "rigorous" cleaning process first, and personnel checked for the presence of whales and dolphins before the live-firing exercise started.Other warships, including an aircraft carrier in 2006, have been deliberately sunk at sea by the US as part of training and to create artificial reefs for marine life.Image source, US Naval Forces Europe-AfricaImage caption, A 43-year-old frigate was used for target practiceThe former guided missile frigate was struck by a missile from USS Paul Ignatius and a torpedo from USS Massachusetts as part of Exercise Atlantic Thunder 2026.The UK's Royal Navy also tested "ship-busting" weapons during the exercise.HMS Portland, a Type 23 frigate, fired a Naval Sea Missile (NSM) - an advanced sea skimming weapon that can travel close to supersonic speeds and hit a target more than100 miles away. The ship's Wildcat helicopter also fired Sea Venom missiles at the target. The Royal Navy said it was the first live firing of the weapons from a Wildcat helicopter at a realistic target.USS Klakring entered service in 1983 and was decommissioned in 2013.It was named after Rear Adm Thomas B Klakring, who was awarded three US Navy Crosses as the commander of a submarine during World War Two.Image source, US Naval Forces Europe-AfricaImage caption, USS Klakring was hit by a missile and torpedo during Exercise Atlantic ThunderThe US Navy said sinking exercises were prepared in strict compliance with environmental regulations.A spokesperson said: "The extensive preparations for the exercise include putting the hulk through a rigorous cleaning process to remove contaminants and old equipment, thereby assuring that the environmental impact of the exercise is minimal. "Sinking ex-navy vessels, which are specially prepared as targets, provides a practicable method for conducting large scale exercises of this type, to train at the high level required by the armed forces."

schema.headline: 'Ship buster' missiles sink old US warship in live fire training off Scotland

title: Mauricio Pochettino on Man City charges: 'We lived through period of deception'
description: Former Tottenham and Chelsea manager Mauricio Pochettino says "we have lived through a period of deception" after Manchester City were found guilty of
body: Former Tottenham and Chelsea manager Mauricio Pochettino says "we have lived through a period of deception" after Manchester City were found guilty of breaking the majority of the charges brought against them by the Premier League.An independent panel found City to be guilty of a wide range of financial rule breaches, with the Athletic, external reporting on Friday that 114 of the 115 charges against them have been upheld. Sanctions are yet to be announced, but City plan on appealing against the decision. The charges relate to a period from 2009-10 to 2017-18, while they were accused of a failure to co-operate with Premier League investigations between December 2018 to February 2023.United States manager Pochettino managed three clubs in the Premier League during that time, with the 54-year-old spending 15 months at Southampton, five years at Tottenham and a single season with Chelsea. "Whatever punishment [they choose], it's impossible to turn back time," said Pochettino. "It's done a lot of damage. Many clubs followed the rules and some didn't. "Maybe they thought that the punishment [wouldn't come for a lot of years] - what are they going to do? An economic punishment? Docking points? It's really hard."It is a huge sadness. We get into a situation where what got celebrated wasn't that real, what seemed good maybe wasn't so good, what didn't look good maybe was good but couldn't be good because of what happened. "We went through something where sporting fairness didn't exist. So, how do you repair everything that was damaged because of that, if it's true all of the 114 rules that were broken, we've lived through a period of deception."Earlier this month, Pochettino said Chelsea should be stripped of the 2016-17 Premier League title after being found guilty of historical rule breaches and that it should be "awarded" to his Tottenham side, who finished runners-up. Sources have told BBC Sport that other top flight clubs are seeking legal advice over possible compensation claims following the decision against City. City were charged by the Premier League in February 2023 following a four-year investigation.The club were referred to an independent commission. A behind-closed-doors hearing began in September 2024 and ran for about 12 weeks."Where were the controls?" said Pochettino on City being found guilty. "That's what gets my attention. Where were the controls?"If I remember being at Southampton, then Tottenham - I remember building [the Tottenham Hotspur Stadium] and not having the economic possibility of a transfer for 18 months. "I think we were the only team in the history of the Premier League with 18 months without [making a transfer]."Tottenham was fighting for titles with those above us and every year in the top four, getting to the semi-finals of the Champions League without being able to do a transfer for 18 months, all because we needed to get used to the [Premier League financial controls]? "They were so strict with us but also so lenient with others. Because of that, that's why I say: it's all very strange."

schema.headline: Mauricio Pochettino on Man City charges: 'We lived through period of deception'

title: What Trump's potential US diesel export ban could mean for you
description: Image source, Getty ImagesByFrancisco VelasquezBusiness reporterUS President Donald Trump has said he would back a ban on diesel producers selling ove
body: Image source, Getty ImagesByFrancisco VelasquezBusiness reporterUS President Donald Trump has said he would back a ban on diesel producers selling overseas as surging fuel prices hit drivers ahead of the midterm elections. Diesel prices are hovering near a record $6.45 per gallon on average, according to the American Automobile Association (AAA), due to the ongoing US-Israel war with Iran and tight global supplies.Trump and his backers say a US diesel export ban would protect domestic consumers from those rising costs, but experts say it could trigger major economic waves both at home and across the world if it were to happen.How much diesel does the US produce and export?The US is one of the world's leading energy producers, with domestic refineries churning out roughly four to five million barrels of diesel every day, according to the US Energy Information Administration (EIA).Americans consume about 3.6 million barrels of that daily output. Refiners export the remaining1.2 to 1.5 million barrels per day, making the US a vital supplier to the global market. Between 60% and 70% of this exported fuel goes to Latin America. Nations like Mexico, Brazil, Chile, and Ecuador depend heavily on American shipments to power their transport, farming, and factory sectors. Significant volumes also head across the Atlantic to European countries like France, the Netherlands, and the UK, as buyers search for alternatives to Middle Eastern supplies. What has happened to diesel prices in the US and abroad? US diesel prices have climbed to a record high of over $6.50 per gallon – up nearly 70% year-on-year. The spike has been driven by broader energy market shocks tied to ongoing conflict with Iran, which has restricted critical shipping routes through the Strait of Hormuz, a waterway south of Iran through which one fifth of the world's oil and gas usually flows. Diesel primarily fuels commercial vehicles in the US – such as freight trucks, farm machinery and cargo trains – which are used for transporting goods and construction. This means higher diesel prices can drive up the price of food, building projects and many other things.Outside the US, diesel is used in both commercial and consumer vehicles, but the effects of higher prices are similar. In the UK, diesel prices at the pump have hit an all-time high, prompting warnings about logistics costs and household budgets.What has Trump said, and what is his argument? Trump suggested over the weekend that restricting or outright banning US diesel exports could keep fuel in the domestic market and drive down prices for American consumers. The president said on Sunday that the administration was "thinking about it very seriously". His comments mirror remarks made on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly, where he stated that he had called to "not send out the diesel". Trump argues that keeping those extra barrels in the US would lower pump prices, offering immediate relief to drivers, truckers, and businesses ahead of the midterm elections. Supporters, including key Republican lawmakers like Congresswoman Ashley Hinson and Senator Dan Sullivan, view the strategy as an effective way to shield the domestic economy from foreign shocks, arguing that American energy should serve American workers first. What would an export ban mean for the US and the rest of the world? For the US economy, a ban could deliver short-term relief at the pump by flooding the domestic market with excess supply. However, energy analysts warn it could backfire. David Fyfe, chief economist at Argus Media, notes that cutting off American supply would likely cause international prices to skyrocket. That would push up global freight, food, and industrial costs, ultimately "feeding inflation back into the global economy". "At a stroke, the US's reputation as a reliable supplier of energy to the world would be shot," Fyfe added. Removing more than a million barrels of daily American supply would trigger a fierce bidding war among importing nations in Latin America and Europe. Sarah Raffoul, analytics manager at Argus Media, noted that while higher international prices would eventually curb demand, the immediate gap would severely strain trade relationships and accelerate global inflation.UK Chancellor John Healey has told BBC News that the UK is in talks with US authorities over a potential diesel export ban and has started preparing for it.Meanwhile, in France and across continental Europe, governments are struggling with similar cost-of-living pressures because of rising fuel prices. schema.headline: What Trump's potential US diesel export ban could mean for you

title: OpenAI scraps rollout of new AI model over safety concerns
description: OpenAI has announced it will not release its latest AI model due to safety concerns.Its GPT-6.1 Astra system, which performs tasks like browsing the w
body: OpenAI has announced it will not release its latest AI model due to safety concerns.Its GPT-6.1 Astra system, which performs tasks like browsing the web and using apps by itself, "didn't quite meet the bar" of the company's standards, according to Saachi Jain, head of safety systems at OpenAI.The ChatGPT-maker also issued an update on incidents that occurred in June but were not made public until last week, where its models accessed Australian government websites and systems without authorisation.It comes as breaches by major AI firms' models intensify the debate about risks posed by the tech - with Anthropic underlining its concerns AI might threaten humanity as it prepares to go public.Reuters reported on Tuesday that the AI developer - which makes ChatGPT-rival Claude - plans to warn potential investors in its Initial Public Offering (IPO) that the tech may pose "catastrophic or existential risks to humanity", according to a prospectus it has seen, external.Despite the stark warnings, the company is expected to become one of the most valuable in the world when it goes public."I think it's kind of crazy that companies are continuing to push forward with developing these capabilities when we've already seen over the last couple of months of incidents that they're nowhere near safe and controlled enough", said Jess Whittlestone, a senior advisor on AI policy for the Centre for Long-Term Resilience think tank.Top AI leaders including Anthropic boss Dario Amodei and OpenAI's Sam Altman have urged the industry to slow the pace of development.OpenAI's decision, first reported by the Wall Street Journal, is a rare instance of a major AI developer pulling a new release over safety concerns.The model fell short in terms of "staying within scope and authorisation and how it communicates back to the user about the type of work it's done," Jain said."We want to make sure our model development is safe no matter whether that's in the company, or when we ship it to users. But when we ship it to users, we have an extremely high bar in terms of safety and alignment," she added.The flagship GPT-6 Astra agentic model was released in September and specialises in complex reasoning and executing tasks autonomously. OpenAI said it was the result of "years of research and big bets".OpenAI is set to hold its annual DevDay developer conference in San Francisco on Tuesday, where it is expected to make several announcements. It is unclear if a new version of Astra will be among them.The company's security controls have come under intense scrutiny after several high-profile incidents involving its technology.It is not the first time a large AI developer has pulled or held back a new model.Earlier this year, Anthropic said it would not publicly release a powerful Claude model, Mythos, because it was too good at finding dormant software bugs.The company released a version of that model to the public several months later.OpenAI meanwhile said in 2019 it would not be "too dangerous" to release one of its GPT models, now used to power its tools like ChatGPT.The firm's decision to not publicly release the latest version of Astra was "a welcome sign that they are taking safety concerns seriously," said Prof Tony Cohn, foundational models theme lead at the Alan Turing Institute.But he added that "safety should not be left purely in the hands of the developers: it should also be monitored and verified through independent government-approved regulators".Prof Gina Neff, of the Minderoo Centre for Technology and Democracy at the University of Cambridge, said OpenAI's announcement showed "how much more the company needs to do to make their AI products safe".She told the BBC it was "critical" to have independent tests of AI models by labs like the UK's AI Security Institute - which evaluates frontier systems on a voluntary basis - because "these companies have proven that we can't rely solely on them for our safety".OpenAI added that it will develop "practical approaches" to how developers and governments identify and disclose future AI incidents.The company will fund cyber security measures, offer dedicated support to impacted agencies and set up a taskforce to manage the risks from increasingly advanced AI agents.It also said a top OpenAI executive would attend a Joint Select Committee hearing on AI in Australia on 6 October.In July, OpenAI said its AI systems had accessed the internet and hacked into open-source developer hub Hugging Face, prompting researchers and officials to call for tighter controls over the technology.On Monday, chip giant Nvidia released a set of software safety tools for autonomous AI platforms - called agents - that it said could have prevented the Hugging Face hack.One of the new tools uses hardware features in Nvidia's chips to contain agents.  Nvidia boss Jensen Huang has largely dismissed calls for tighter AI regulations, arguing that rogue agents are an engineering problem that can be solved.Nvidia agreed to buy Hugging Face for $12.9bn (£9.74bn) earlier this month.

title: Liverpool: Inside the club's increasing global investment in youth
description: Liverpool may have made three signings worth more than £100m each over the past two summers in Florian Wirtz, Alexander Isak and Bradley Barcola, but
body: Liverpool may have made three signings worth more than £100m each over the past two summers in Florian Wirtz, Alexander Isak and Bradley Barcola, but internally there is a realisation that after a significant amount of young talent was sold last summer, the club need to replenish that talent pool.Since 2020, Liverpool have made more than £230m from selling players who have represented them at youth level and that has been a major part of owner Fenway Sports Group's self-sustaining business model, with the funds reinvested into the club.Since Brexit, there is a 'premium' on young English players and it is why Liverpool's global talent department, led by Matt Newberry since the winter of 2024, now have a major role to play.Fifa rules state that international transfers of players are only permitted if the player is over 18 and, since Brexit, Premier League clubs are no longer permitted to sign players under 18 from European countries.Newberry's team is responsible for deciding which young talents from overseas should be targeted for a move. Using their wealth of contacts across the world, including dedicated regional scouts, Liverpool are becoming increasingly aggressive in the space. It helps that new sporting director Julian Ward is well known for his global network. "Any player we sign, the first intention is that we want them to play in the first team and there's a belief that there's a chance for everyone that signs here," Alex Inglethorpe, Liverpool Academy director told BBC Sport."That really is no different since the impact of Brexit on the English market, which is quite significant. There's now a premium on young English players. Time will tell if that premium is worthwhile but it's definitely a change."So it's fairly natural for a club like Liverpool to look within Merseyside in the first instance then broaden that out - national recruitment happens at 14 and after that you look globally, which is what we've done." Mor Talla Ndiaye's journey began in the Senegalese village of Sandiara where he played football in the streets.He progressed through the ranks playing for Bousports Academy in the town of Thiadiaye before joining Amitie Football Club in the city of Thies. Come January this year, Liverpool fended off interest from other European clubs and signed the 18-year-old for about £1m plus add-ons."You have access to certain talent based on points accrued from playing homegrown players. We had a couple of ESC (elite significant contribution) spots to explore the wider market and that's something which, even prior to Brexit, was a fairly normal thing," Inglethorpe adds.Ndiaye is a left-footed centre-half who played for Liverpool in pre-season under Andoni Iraola and was an unused substitute in three games in the second half of last season under Arne Slot."He's an incredible story, isn't he? From where he's come from to where he is - and he's such a humble kid. He's an unbelievable lad to work with," Rob Page, Liverpool's U21 boss, told BBC Sport."There's exciting times ahead but he's got a lot of work to do. He's nowhere near the finished article but he's on the right path. His attitude is spot on and he's at the club that will definitely help him develop."At Liverpool, there is an optimism regarding Ndiaye and a genuine belief that if he makes it to the top, it could be one of the great football stories.  Liverpool opened discussions with his academy and his agency, Sport Cover, after scouts spotted his performances at the U17 World Cup in Qatar last winter and several video calls were arranged before the club's representatives travelled to Senegal.Once there, they visited where Ndiaye trained, as well as meeting the people that supported his development before presenting their vision to him directly.A round-table meeting was organised with his family to help understand his environment, the story and the context in which he grew up.Ultimately, Ndiaye chose Liverpool because they offered the clearest pathway and their approach in getting to know him stood out. Ndiaye isn't the only player to have been identified and recruited by Liverpool's global talent team.After the U17 World Cup, Liverpool also made a £2.6m move for another centre-half, Ifeanyi Ndukwe.Ndukwe was impressive in pre-season and the 18-year-old Austrian has gone on loan to Levante in La Liga as he looks to obtain a UK work permit. The list doesn't stop there. Samuel Martinez, the 17-year-old Colombian midfielder, will join next summer after having "30 offers from around the world, external", according to his father. It doesn't always work. Arsenal beat Liverpool to the signing of Andria Bartishvili from Georgia last month and the 17-year-old will join the Gunners next summer when he is 18.But the moves for Martinez and Ndiaye showcase Liverpool's willingness to spread beyond Europe and into areas they may not have explored before. Given the inevitability of other top clubs circling emerging talent, the idea of selling the pathway that Liverpool offers is imperative.Since arriving, Ndiaye has settled in with a host family - which is normal when players aren't from the area - that are used to working with Liverpool."Players come from varying parts of the world and, when someone comes in and doesn't speak much English at the start, you have to help with that and help understand culturally the differences in food, the weather and even the pitches you play on," Inglethorpe said."There's a lot of understanding in terms of the level of support that's needed and the most important thing you can give a young player is the time. "I'm delighted that Mor made such a strong impression and he's done as well as he has, but we hope that he's going to get better and better as he continues to adapt."This summer, Liverpool also confirmed moves for Lucca Brughmans, the 18-year-old Belgian goalkeeper, and Djylian N'Guessan, the 18-year-old French forward, with both set to join the club permanently in 2027. In the modern game, most talents are known and there aren't many hidden gems anymore, but Liverpool believe that by digging deeper and wider they can get ahead of the curve, using their global network and their reputation as a club that will help players develop.

title: Could psychedelic therapy become NHS treatment for mental health?
description: From Amazon retreats to clinical research: The rise of psychedelic therapyImage caption, Claire Torpey attended retreats in Central and South America
body: From Amazon retreats to clinical research: The rise of psychedelic therapyImage caption, Claire Torpey attended retreats in Central and South America where participants legally take psychedelics as part of guided therapeutic programmesByCollette HoweNorth East and CumbriaFrom retreats in the Amazon to clinical trials in Newcastle, psychedelic therapy is attracting growing attention as a possible treatment for depression. Could hallucinogenic drugs one day become part of mainstream NHS care?Claire Torpey had tried traditional forms of mental health support, including counselling. But she says there was still something she could not shake."There was a deep sadness. I was living in chronic anxiety," she says.Claire, from Tynemouth, North Tyneside, spent part of her childhood in care and says the challenges she faced growing up were compounded by the deaths of her father and grandmother in consecutive years."There wasn't anything that was really moving the needle from my internal state. I was deeply sad and I didn't want to be here."Image source, Getty images/ Mark Fox PhotographyImage caption, Ayahuasca is a traditional Amazonian brew containing the psychedelic compound DMTSeeking alternatives, Claire travelled to South and Central America to attend retreats where participants legally take psychedelics as part of guided therapeutic programmes.The retreats involved psilocybin, the psychoactive compound found in magic mushrooms, and ayahuasca, a traditional Amazonian brew containing the psychedelic compound DMT.Psychedelic tourism has grown in popularity, but experts warn that unethical and unregulated practices can pose serious risks. There have been reports of participants dying after attending retreats and ceremonies abroad.For Claire, however, she says the experience was transformative."It wasn't until I started taking these medicines that it started to lift," she says."I started to find a place of peace and happiness. It took me on a journey of forgiveness."I don't believe that normal talk therapies would have got me there."'Does not turn off depression'In the UK, psilocybin and DMT are Class A drugs and are classified as Schedule 1 substances, meaning they are considered to have no recognised medicinal use.Yet interest in psychedelic-assisted therapy is growing.At Newcastle's Care Pathway Enhancement (CaPE) Clinic, run by Cumbria, Northumberland, Tyne and Wear NHS Foundation Trust, researchers are investigating whether psilocybin could help treat conditions including depression.Image caption, Participants to the clinical trial are given psilocybin in capsule formThe theory is that, when used in a controlled setting, psychedelics can help people process difficult thoughts and emotions. Some researchers liken the mind to a snow globe: the drugs temporarily disrupt established thought patterns, allowing thoughts and feelings to settle differently and providing new perspectives on past experiences.Consultant psychiatrist Dr Mourad Wahba, who leads the research, says participants often report significant shifts in how they view themselves and their experiences."The idea is that through having this experience, people can change their behaviours and patterns of thinking," he says.Image caption, Lead researcher Dr Mourad Wahba says obtaining licences to work with Schedule 1 substances can significantly delay studiesThe treatment involves extensive preparation and support before and after dosing sessions.Clinical psychologist Tom Sharp helps facilitate the trials. Participants receive psilocybin in capsule form before spending up to eight hours in a specially designed dosing room under the supervision of therapists."People can develop a sense of what might have caused their depression," he says.Researchers are keen to temper expectations."This type of work isn't some silver bullet," says Sharp. "It doesn't turn off depression."Wahba agrees. While early findings are encouraging, he says larger studies are still needed to establish how effective the treatments are and whether any benefits can be sustained in the longer term.Image caption, Participants can spend up to eight hours in a specially designed dosing room under the supervision of therapistsThe Royal College of Psychiatrists has backed further research into psychedelic-assisted therapy.Dr David Cousins, chair of its psychopharmacology committee, said: "The College supports further research into psychedelics such as psilocybin, which have the potential to help in the treatment of people with conditions such as depression, including those who are less responsive to other forms of care."Some researchers believe psychedelic-assisted therapy may offer longer-lasting benefits for certain patients by helping them address underlying thoughts, emotions and behaviours rather than simply managing symptoms.However, Cousins cautioned against seeking treatment outside regulated settings."We strongly advise against people self-medicating or seeking access to unregulated treatments as there are risks in doing so."Supporters stress that psychedelic therapy is very different from recreational drug use. In clinical settings, participants are screened, monitored and supported before, during and after treatment.'I became quite desperate'Some UK charities and organisations are also helping people access psychedelic therapy overseas.Keith John Abraham, founder of Heroic Hearts Project UK, helps former military personnel attend retreats involving ayahuasca to support conditions such as post-traumatic stress disorder."Most people come out of this and feel like they've got a renewed sense of energy and purpose," he says.Abraham, an army veteran, turned to psychedelic therapy after struggling with the effects of military service."Afghanistan came at a great personal cost to me."I went down the traditional avenues and I found they didn't work for me and became quite desperate."Image source, suppliedImage caption, Keith J Abraham said he turned to psychedelic therapy after struggling with the effects of military serviceAbraham says psychedelic therapy helped him make significant progress, but warns against portraying it as a miracle cure."We shouldn't come into this assuming that all of our problems will be resolved. But life can be very much improved."Abraham describes psychedelic therapy as the "future of mental health care".Robin Daly, founder of the cancer charity Yes to Life, believes psychedelic-assisted therapy could also help some people cope with the emotional impact of serious illness.He says a cancer diagnosis can leave people confronting questions about mortality, purpose and the future, and that psilocybin may help some patients come to terms with that reality."It's not about going off into la-la land," he says."It's about being able to accommodate the fact, 'OK, I'm in this situation, I have cancer', but to put it in a much bigger context."While stressing that psilocybin is not a cure for cancer, he describes its potential impact on some patients as "revolutionary".He believes access should not be limited to people who can afford to travel overseas for treatment.'Giving patients a choice'Researchers argue progress is being slowed by regulation.Wahba says obtaining licences to work with Schedule 1 substances can significantly delay studies."Let's say I start talking about a study in June. We apply for the licence in June or July. We might not get the licence until January," he says."So far, the risks aren't as pronounced as we would see with a lot of other medications. It just seems quite prohibitive at this point."Looking ahead, he hopes psychedelic-assisted therapy could one day sit alongside existing NHS treatments."Giving patients choice is number one. So, it being part of our menu would be the ideal scenario for me."The Home Office says it is considering advice on reducing barriers to research involving controlled drugs while ensuring safeguards remain in place.The UK's Medicines and Healthcare products Regulatory Agency says it facilitates clinical research, but it is still too early to know whether psychedelic treatments might one day become routinely available.Follow BBC North East on X, external, Facebook, external, Nextdoor and Instagram, external and listen to Radio Newcastle on BBC Sounds.
